title: Avoiding deconditioning in hospital when you have arthritis (UK)
meta_title: Hospital Deconditioning and Arthritis: Staying Strong
meta_description: How time in bed during a hospital stay can weaken older people with arthritis and frailty, and what you and your family can do to stay active and recover.
excerpt: How time in bed during a hospital stay can weaken older people with arthritis and frailty, and what you and your family can do to stay active and recover.
direct_answer: Deconditioning is the loss of strength, stamina and independence that can happen quickly with bed rest in hospital, especially if you are older or frail. Getting up, dressed and moving as soon as it is safe, eating and drinking well, and doing simple bed and chair exercises can help.

content:
Staying in bed for long periods in hospital can quickly weaken muscles, stiffen joints and reduce confidence, especially if you already live with arthritis and frailty. This is called deconditioning, and it can make it harder to go home and manage as before.

This guide explains why it happens and what you and your family can do, working with the ward team. It is educational information. Always follow the advice of the staff caring for you.

Why it happens

Muscles weaken with inactivity, and older people lose strength faster and regain it more slowly. Arthritis can make joints stiffer after rest. Being unwell, in pain or confused can also make it harder to move.

What helps

  • Get up, dressed in your own clothes and sitting out in a chair when it is safe to do so.
  • Walk to the toilet or bathroom with help if needed, rather than staying in bed.
  • Use your usual glasses, hearing aids, walking aid and well-fitting shoes or slippers.
  • Eat and drink well, including protein, and ask for help if opening packets is hard.
  • Keep a normal routine of day and night, and keep your mind active.

Simple bed and chair exercises

If a physiotherapist agrees, try gentle exercises several times a day:

  • Ankle pumps: point and flex your feet.
  • Knee straightening: tighten your thigh and press the back of your knee down.
  • Buttock squeezes.
  • Arm raises and hand squeezes.
  • Sit-to-stand practice from a chair, with help if needed.

Arthritis medicines in hospital

Bring all your medicines or a list. Tell staff about arthritis medicines, especially steroids, which should not be stopped suddenly, and medicines that affect immunity, which may be paused during infection on medical advice.

How family can help

  • Bring day clothes, shoes, glasses and hearing aids.
  • Encourage walking and sitting out, following staff advice.
  • Tell staff what the person could do before admission.

After discharge

Recovery may continue at home. Reablement or intermediate care can help rebuild strength and independence.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is bed rest good for recovery?

Some rest is needed when very unwell, but long periods in bed can cause weakness. Ask staff when you can safely get up.

What if I am in too much pain to move?

Tell staff. Good pain relief should help you move.

Can I bring my own walking aid?

Usually yes. Ask a physiotherapist to check it.
